title: Motion in a Straight Line
description: Class 11 Physics Motion in a Straight Line: position, displacement, velocity, acceleration, equations of motion, x-t and v-t graphs, free fall and relative velocity with solved numericals and tests.

topics.title: Position, Distance & Displacement
topics.concept:
Mechanics begins with kinematics — the description of motion without asking what causes it. The simplest case is motion along a single straight line, called rectilinear motion or motion in one dimension. To describe even this we must first agree on a way to say where an object is, which is why every problem starts with a frame of reference.

A frame of reference is a coordinate system attached to an observer, together with a clock. For 1D motion we draw a single axis (usually the $x$-axis), pick an origin $O$ as the zero mark, and choose a positive direction. The position of a particle is then a single number $x$ — positive on one side of the origin, negative on the other. A car standing at $x = +200\,\text{m}$ and another at $x = -150\,\text{m}$ are on opposite sides of $O$. The same motion looks different in different frames: a ball dropped inside a moving train falls straight down for a passenger but follows a curved path for someone on the platform.

As a particle moves, two quantities describe how far it has gone. The path length (or distance) is the total length of the actual path travelled. It is a scalar, is always positive, and never decreases. The displacement $\Delta x = x_2 - x_1$ is the change in position — the straight gap from start to finish with a sign that tells the direction. In one dimension a vector is fully captured by this sign: $+$ means one way, $-$ the other. So displacement is a vector in 1D, while path length is a scalar.

The two are equal in size only when motion is in a single direction without reversing. The moment a particle turns back, path length keeps growing while the magnitude of displacement may shrink. A boy who walks from $x = 0$ to $x = 60\,\text{m}$ and back to $x = 20\,\text{m}$ covers a path length of $60 + 40 = 100\,\text{m}$, but his displacement is only $+20\,\text{m}$. Thus path length $\ge |\Delta x|$ always.

Motion is called uniform when the particle covers equal displacements in equal intervals of time, however small the interval. Otherwise it is non-uniform. A metro coasting on a clear track is close to uniform; the same metro pulling out of a station is non-uniform.

  • Frame of reference: origin + axis + clock; chosen before describing any motion.
  • Position $x$: a signed number; sign shows side of origin.
  • Path length: total path travelled; scalar; always increases.
  • Displacement $\Delta x = x_2 - x_1$: vector in 1D; can be $+$, $-$ or $0$.
  • Always $|\Delta x| \le$ path length; equal only if direction never reverses.

examples.problem: A particle moves along the $x$-axis from $x_1 = -4\,\text{m}$ to $x_2 = +12\,\text{m}$. Find its displacement.
examples.solution:
1. Displacement $\Delta x = x_2 - x_1$.
  2. $\Delta x = 12 - (-4) = 12 + 4 = 16\,\text{m}$.
  3. The sign is positive, so the shift is along the $+x$ direction.

Answer: $\Delta x = +16\,\text{m}$ (along $+x$).

examples.problem: A boy walks from $x = 0$ to $x = 70\,\text{m}$ and then returns to $x = 25\,\text{m}$. Find the path length and the displacement.
examples.solution:
1. Forward path $= 70\,\text{m}$; return path $= 70 - 25 = 45\,\text{m}$.
  2. Path length $= 70 + 45 = 115\,\text{m}$.
  3. Displacement $= x_{final} - x_{initial} = 25 - 0 = 25\,\text{m}$.

Answer: Path length $= 115\,\text{m}$, Displacement $= +25\,\text{m}$.

examples.problem: A runner completes one full lap of a $400\,\text{m}$ straight-and-curved track and stops at the start. State the path length and the displacement.
examples.solution:
1. One full lap means the actual path travelled $= 400\,\text{m}$.
  2. The start and end points coincide.
  3. Displacement $= $ shortest gap between identical points $= 0$.

Answer: Path length $= 400\,\text{m}$, Displacement $= 0$.

examples.problem: Two cars are at positions $x_A = +320\,\text{m}$ and $x_B = -180\,\text{m}$ on a straight road. How far apart are they?
examples.solution:
1. Separation $= |x_A - x_B|$.
  2. $= |320 - (-180)| = |320 + 180|$.
  3. $= 500\,\text{m}$.

Answer: The cars are $500\,\text{m}$ apart.

examples.problem: In successive equal intervals of $2\,\text{s}$, a body covers displacements $6\,\text{m}, 6\,\text{m}, 6\,\text{m}$ along $+x$. Is the motion uniform? Find the total displacement.
examples.solution:
1. Equal displacements ($6\,\text{m}$) occur in equal intervals ($2\,\text{s}$).
  2. By definition, this is uniform motion.
  3. Total displacement $= 6 + 6 + 6 = 18\,\text{m}$.

Answer: Uniform motion; total displacement $= 18\,\text{m}$.

examples.problem: A particle starts at $x = 5\,\text{m}$, moves to $x = -3\,\text{m}$, then to $x = 9\,\text{m}$. Find the total path length and the net displacement.
examples.solution:
1. First leg: $|{-3} - 5| = 8\,\text{m}$. Second leg: $|9 - (-3)| = 12\,\text{m}$.
  2. Path length $= 8 + 12 = 20\,\text{m}$.
  3. Net displacement $= x_{final} - x_{initial} = 9 - 5 = 4\,\text{m}$.

Answer: Path length $= 20\,\text{m}$, Displacement $= +4\,\text{m}$.

recap: A frame of reference (origin + axis + clock) must be fixed before describing any motion.
Position $x$ is a signed number; its sign tells which side of the origin the particle is on.
Path length is the total path travelled — a scalar that never decreases.
Displacement $\Delta x = x_2 - x_1$ is a vector in 1D and can be positive, negative or zero.
Path length $\ge |\Delta x|$; they are equal only when the direction of motion never reverses.

quiz.q: A particle moves from $x_1 = -2\,\text{m}$ to $x_2 = 6\,\text{m}$. Its displacement is:
Which statement is always true for motion in a straight line?
options: Displacement is greater than path length
Path length is greater than or equal to the magnitude of displacement
quiz.explanation: Path length is the total path travelled and can never be less than the size of the straight-line displacement.

quiz.q: An object returns to its starting point after moving around. Over the whole trip, its displacement is:
quiz.explanation: Start and end coincide, so the change in position is zero, even though path length is not.

quiz.q: Equal displacements in equal time intervals (however small) define:
quiz.explanation: This is precisely the definition of uniform motion in a straight line.

topics.title: Velocity & Acceleration
topics.concept:
Knowing how far a particle has gone is only half the story; we also want to know how fast and how its motion is changing. Average speed is total path length divided by total time, a scalar: $\text{speed}_{avg} = \dfrac{\text{path length}}{\Delta t}$. Average velocity is total displacement divided by total time, a vector that carries the sign of $\Delta x$: $\bar{v} = \dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{x_2 - x_1}{t_2 - t_1}$. The SI unit of both is $\text{m/s}$, and the handy road conversion is $1\,\text{km/h} = \dfrac{5}{18}\,\text{m/s}$.

Average values hide the moment-to-moment detail. To capture the speedometer reading at one instant we shrink the time interval to zero. The instantaneous velocity is the limit of average velocity as $\Delta t \to 0$, which is exactly the calculus derivative of position with respect to time: $v = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{dx}{dt}$. Geometrically, $v$ is the slope of the tangent to the position-time ($x$-$t$) graph at that instant. The magnitude of instantaneous velocity equals the instantaneous speed.

When velocity itself changes, the particle accelerates. Average acceleration is the change in velocity over the time taken: $\bar{a} = \dfrac{v_2 - v_1}{t_2 - t_1} = \dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$. Pushing $\Delta t \to 0$ gives the instantaneous acceleration, the derivative of velocity: $a = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = \dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}$. Acceleration is a vector and its SI unit is $\text{m/s}^2$. On a velocity-time ($v$-$t$) graph, $a$ is the slope of the curve.

Signs deserve care in 1D. Acceleration is positive when velocity increases in the $+x$ sense and negative when velocity decreases — but a negative acceleration does not always mean slowing down. If a particle already moves in the $-x$ direction, a negative acceleration speeds it up. The reliable rule is: the particle speeds up when $v$ and $a$ have the same sign and slows down (retardation) when they have opposite signs.

A special, very common case is uniform acceleration, where $a$ is constant in both magnitude and direction. Free fall near the Earth's surface (ignoring air) is the classic example, with $a = g \approx 9.8\,\text{m/s}^2$ directed downward. Under uniform acceleration the velocity changes linearly with time, which is what makes the equations of motion in the next topic so simple.

  • Average velocity $\bar{v} = \dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}$ (vector); average speed uses path length (scalar).
  • Instantaneous velocity $v = \dfrac{dx}{dt}$ = slope of the $x$-$t$ tangent.
  • Acceleration $a = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = \dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}$ = slope of the $v$-$t$ graph, unit $\text{m/s}^2$.
  • Speeds up when $v$ and $a$ share a sign; slows down (retardation) when they differ.
  • Uniform acceleration: $a$ constant; velocity changes linearly with time.

examples.problem: A car travels $240\,\text{km}$ in $4\,\text{hours}$ along a straight road. Find its average speed in $\text{km/h}$ and $\text{m/s}$.
A particle's position is $x = 4 + 6t - t^2$ (SI units). Find its velocity at $t = 2\,\text{s}$.
For $x = 4 + 6t - t^2$, find the acceleration and the instant when the velocity becomes zero.
A car accelerates from $u = 5\,\text{m/s}$ to $v = 23\,\text{m/s}$ in $6\,\text{s}$. Find its average acceleration.
A scooter moving at $20\,\text{m/s}$ slows uniformly to rest in $8\,\text{s}$. Find the acceleration and state whether it speeds up or slows down.
examples.solution:
1. $a = \dfrac{v - u}{t} = \dfrac{0 - 20}{8} = -2.5\,\text{m/s}^2$.
  2. Velocity is positive while acceleration is negative — opposite signs.
  3. Opposite signs mean the scooter slows down (retardation).

Answer: $a = -2.5\,\text{m/s}^2$; it slows down (retardation).

examples.problem: A man covers the first half of a straight trip at $30\,\text{km/h}$ and the second half (equal distance) at $60\,\text{km/h}$. Find his average speed for the whole trip.
examples.solution:
1. For equal distances, average speed $= \dfrac{2 v_1 v_2}{v_1 + v_2}$ (harmonic mean).
  2. $= \dfrac{2 \times 30 \times 60}{30 + 60} = \dfrac{3600}{90}$.
  3. $= 40\,\text{km/h}$.

Answer: Average speed $= 40\,\text{km/h}$.

recap: Average velocity $\bar{v} = \dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}$ is a vector; average speed uses path length and is a scalar.
Instantaneous velocity $v = \dfrac{dx}{dt}$ equals the slope of the tangent to the $x$-$t$ graph.
Acceleration $a = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = \dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}$ is the slope of the $v$-$t$ graph; unit $\text{m/s}^2$.
A particle speeds up when $v$ and $a$ have the same sign and slows down when they have opposite signs.
Uniform acceleration means $a$ is constant, so velocity changes linearly with time.

quiz.q: The instantaneous velocity is the slope of which graph?
quiz.explanation: Since $v = \dfrac{dx}{dt}$, the slope of the tangent to the position-time graph gives instantaneous velocity.

quiz.q: For $x = 3t^2$ (SI units), the velocity at $t = 2\,\text{s}$ is:
A body has positive velocity and negative acceleration. The body is:
quiz.explanation: Opposite signs of $v$ and $a$ mean the speed is decreasing — retardation.

quiz.q: The SI unit of acceleration is:
quiz.explanation: Acceleration is change of velocity per unit time, so its unit is $\text{m/s}^2$.

topics.title: Equations of Motion & Graphs
topics.concept:
When acceleration is constant, the messy calculus collapses into three tidy formulas — the kinematic equations. Let $u$ be the initial velocity, $v$ the velocity after time $t$, $a$ the constant acceleration and $s$ the displacement. The three equations are: $v = u + at$, $\;s = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$, and $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$. They are valid only while $a$ is constant.

Each follows from calculus. Since $a = \dfrac{dv}{dt}$ is constant, integrating gives $v = u + at$ — the first equation. Because $v = \dfrac{dx}{dt} = u + at$, integrating again gives $s = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$ — the second equation. Eliminating $t$ between the first two yields $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ — the third equation, the one to reach for whenever time is neither given nor wanted. A useful extra result is the distance in the $n$-th second: $s_n = u + \dfrac{a}{2}(2n - 1)$.

Graphs make motion visible and turn slopes and areas into physics. On a position-time ($x$-$t$) graph, the slope gives velocity: a straight line means uniform velocity, a curve means changing velocity, and a horizontal line means rest. On a velocity-time ($v$-$t$) graph two facts matter at once — the slope gives acceleration, and the area under the graph gives displacement. For uniform acceleration the $v$-$t$ line is straight, and the area beneath it (a trapezium) is exactly $s = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$. This area method is one of the most powerful shortcuts in kinematics.

Free fall is uniformly accelerated motion under gravity alone. Near the Earth's surface every freely falling body has the same downward acceleration $g \approx 9.8\,\text{m/s}^2$ (often taken as $10\,\text{m/s}^2$), independent of mass. Taking the upward direction as positive, we use $a = -g$. For a body dropped from rest, $u = 0$, so $v = -gt$ and $|s| = \dfrac{1}{2}gt^2$. For a body thrown up, it rises until $v = 0$, reaching height $H = \dfrac{u^2}{2g}$, and the time up equals the time down.

Finally, motion is always relative to a frame, so relative velocity in 1D is just a subtraction of signed velocities: the velocity of $A$ with respect to $B$ is $v_{AB} = v_A - v_B$. If two trains move the same way, the faster overtakes the slower at $v_A - v_B$; if they move oppositely, they approach at $v_A - (-v_B) = v_A + v_B$. Getting the signs right is the whole game.

  • First: $v = u + at$. Second: $s = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$. Third: $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$.
  • $x$-$t$ slope $= v$; $v$-$t$ slope $= a$ and area under $v$-$t$ $= s$.
  • Free fall: $a = g \approx 9.8\,\text{m/s}^2$ downward, same for all masses.
  • Max height of an upthrow: $H = \dfrac{u^2}{2g}$; time up $=$ time down.
  • Relative velocity (1D): $v_{AB} = v_A - v_B$ using signed values.

examples.problem: A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at $2\,\text{m/s}^2$ for $10\,\text{s}$. Find its final velocity and the distance covered.
examples.solution:
1. $u = 0,\; a = 2\,\text{m/s}^2,\; t = 10\,\text{s}$.
  2. $v = u + at = 0 + 2(10) = 20\,\text{m/s}$.
  3. $s = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2 = 0 + \dfrac{1}{2}(2)(10)^2 = 100\,\text{m}$.

Answer: $v = 20\,\text{m/s}$, $s = 100\,\text{m}$.

examples.problem: A train moving at $90\,\text{km/h}$ is brought to rest over a distance of $500\,\text{m}$. Find its retardation.
A stone is dropped from rest from a tower and hits the ground in $4\,\text{s}$. Find the height of the tower. (Take $g = 9.8\,\text{m/s}^2$.)
examples.solution:
1. $u = 0,\; a = g = 9.8\,\text{m/s}^2,\; t = 4\,\text{s}$.
  2. $h = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}gt^2 = 0 + \dfrac{1}{2}(9.8)(4)^2$.
  3. $= \dfrac{1}{2}(9.8)(16) = 78.4\,\text{m}$.

Answer: Height of the tower $= 78.4\,\text{m}$.

examples.problem: A ball is thrown vertically up with $u = 20\,\text{m/s}$. Find the maximum height reached. (Take $g = 10\,\text{m/s}^2$.)
examples.solution:
1. At maximum height $v = 0$; take up as positive so $a = -g = -10\,\text{m/s}^2$.
  2. $v^2 = u^2 + 2as \Rightarrow 0 = 20^2 + 2(-10)H$.
  3. $0 = 400 - 20H \Rightarrow H = \dfrac{400}{20} = 20\,\text{m}$.

Answer: Maximum height $H = 20\,\text{m}$.

examples.problem: The $v$-$t$ graph of a body is a straight line from $u = 4\,\text{m/s}$ at $t = 0$ to $v = 16\,\text{m/s}$ at $t = 6\,\text{s}$. Use the area to find the displacement.
examples.solution:
1. Displacement = area under the $v$-$t$ line = area of a trapezium.
  2. Area $= \dfrac{1}{2}(u + v)\,t = \dfrac{1}{2}(4 + 16)(6)$.
  3. $= \dfrac{1}{2}(20)(6) = 60\,\text{m}$.

Answer: Displacement $= 60\,\text{m}$.

examples.problem: Two cars move in the same direction on a straight road at $20\,\text{m/s}$ and $14\,\text{m/s}$. Find the velocity of the faster car relative to the slower one, and the time it takes to gain a lead of $90\,\text{m}$.
examples.solution:
1. Relative velocity $v_{AB} = v_A - v_B = 20 - 14 = 6\,\text{m/s}$.
  2. Time to gain $90\,\text{m}$: $t = \dfrac{\text{gap}}{v_{AB}} = \dfrac{90}{6}$.
  3. $= 15\,\text{s}$.

Answer: Relative velocity $= 6\,\text{m/s}$; time $= 15\,\text{s}$.

recap: The three equations for constant $a$: $v = u + at$, $s = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$, $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$.
On an $x$-$t$ graph the slope is velocity; a straight line means uniform velocity.
On a $v$-$t$ graph the slope is acceleration and the area under it is displacement.
In free fall every body has the same downward acceleration $g \approx 9.8\,\text{m/s}^2$, regardless of mass.
Relative velocity in 1D is $v_{AB} = v_A - v_B$ using signed velocities.

quiz.q: Which equation should you use when time is neither given nor asked for?
quiz.explanation: $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ contains $u, v, a, s$ but not $t$, so it is the time-free equation.

quiz.q: The area under a velocity-time graph gives:
quiz.explanation: The area between the $v$-$t$ curve and the time axis equals the displacement of the body.

quiz.q: A stone dropped from rest falls for $3\,\text{s}$. Its velocity just before impact is (take $g = 10\,\text{m/s}^2$):
Two cars approach each other at $15\,\text{m/s}$ and $9\,\text{m/s}$. Their relative speed of approach is:
quiz.explanation: For opposite directions the magnitudes add: $15 + 9 = 24\,\text{m/s}$.

online.title: Motion in a Straight Line — Online Test

questions.q: Displacement of a particle in straight-line motion is a:
questions.explanation: Displacement has magnitude and direction (a sign in 1D), so it is a vector.

questions.q: A particle moves from x = 3 m to x = -5 m. Its displacement is:
questions.explanation: $\Delta x = -5 - 3 = -8\,\text{m}$, directed along $-x$.

questions.q: Path length compared with the magnitude of displacement is always:
questions.explanation: Path length can never be less than the size of the straight-line displacement.

questions.q: Instantaneous velocity is defined as:
questions.explanation: Instantaneous velocity is the time derivative of position, $v = \dfrac{dx}{dt}$.

questions.q: The slope of a velocity-time graph gives:
questions.explanation: Slope of the $v$-$t$ graph is $\dfrac{dv}{dt} = a$, the acceleration.

questions.q: For x = 5t^2 (SI), the acceleration is:
questions.explanation: $v = 10t$ and $a = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = 10\,\text{m/s}^2$ (constant).

questions.q: A car accelerates from 4 m/s to 28 m/s in 8 s. Its acceleration is:
36 km/h equals:
questions.explanation: $36 \times \dfrac{5}{18} = 10\,\text{m/s}$.

questions.q: A body starts from rest with a = 4 m/s$^2$. Distance covered in 5 s is:
Which equation does not contain time t?
questions.explanation: $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ relates velocities, acceleration and displacement without $t$.

questions.q: A stone dropped from rest falls for 2 s. Its speed on hitting the ground is (g = 10 m/s$^2$):
questions.explanation: $v = u + gt = 0 + 10 \times 2 = 20\,\text{m/s}$.

questions.q: A ball thrown up with 40 m/s reaches a maximum height of (g = 10 m/s$^2$):
The area under a velocity-time graph between two instants gives the:
questions.explanation: Area under the $v$-$t$ curve equals the displacement over that interval.

questions.q: A body has positive velocity and negative acceleration. It is:
questions.explanation: Opposite signs of $v$ and $a$ mean retardation — the body slows down.

questions.q: Two cars move toward each other at 12 m/s and 8 m/s. Their relative speed of approach is:
questions.explanation: For opposite directions, speeds add: $12 + 8 = 20\,\text{m/s}$.

questions.q: A position-time graph that is a straight line sloping upward represents:
questions.explanation: Constant slope of the $x$-$t$ graph means constant (uniform) velocity.

questions.q: The acceleration due to gravity for a freely falling body is:
questions.explanation: Ignoring air resistance, all bodies fall with the same $g$ regardless of mass.

questions.q: A train slows from 30 m/s to rest in 250 m. Its retardation is:
questions.explanation: $v^2 = u^2 + 2as \Rightarrow 0 = 900 + 2a(250) \Rightarrow a = -1.8\,\text{m/s}^2$.

questions.q: The distance covered by a body starting from rest in the n-th second is proportional to:
questions.explanation: $s_n = u + \dfrac{a}{2}(2n - 1)$; with $u = 0$ it is proportional to $(2n - 1)$.

questions.q: A v-t graph is a horizontal line above the time axis. This means the body has:
questions.explanation: A horizontal $v$-$t$ line means velocity is constant and acceleration (its slope) is zero.

imo.title: Motion in a Straight Line — Olympiad Test

questions.q: A particle's position is x = 2t^3 - 9t^2 + 12t (SI). At what time is its velocity zero (smallest positive t)?
questions.explanation: $v = 6t^2 - 18t + 12 = 6(t-1)(t-2)$; zero at $t = 1\,\text{s}$ and $t = 2\,\text{s}$, smallest is $1\,\text{s}$.

questions.q: A car covers the first half of a distance at 20 m/s and the second half at 30 m/s. Its average speed is:
questions.explanation: Equal distances: $v_{avg} = \dfrac{2 v_1 v_2}{v_1 + v_2} = \dfrac{2 \times 20 \times 30}{50} = 24\,\text{m/s}$.

questions.q: A ball thrown up returns to the thrower in 6 s. The initial speed was (g = 10 m/s$^2$):
questions.explanation: Time of flight $T = \dfrac{2u}{g} \Rightarrow u = \dfrac{gT}{2} = \dfrac{10 \times 6}{2} = 30\,\text{m/s}$.

questions.q: A body starts from rest with uniform acceleration. The ratio of distances covered in the 1st, 2nd and 3rd seconds is:
questions.explanation: Distances in successive seconds go as $(2n - 1)$: $1 : 3 : 5$.

questions.q: A stone is dropped from a balloon ascending at 10 m/s when at height 60 m. Time to reach the ground is (g = 10 m/s$^2$):
questions.explanation: Taking down positive with initial velocity $-10$: $60 = -10t + 5t^2 \Rightarrow t^2 - 2t - 12 = 0 \Rightarrow t = 1 + \sqrt{13} \approx 4\,\text{s}$.

questions.q: Two trains 120 m and 80 m long move toward each other at 15 m/s and 10 m/s. Time to completely cross each other is:
questions.explanation: Relative speed $= 25\,\text{m/s}$; total length $= 200\,\text{m}$; $t = \dfrac{200}{25} = 8\,\text{s}$.

questions.q: The displacement of a body is zero but the distance is not. The body has:
questions.explanation: Zero displacement with non-zero path length means it came back to the starting point.

questions.q: A v-t graph is a straight line passing through the origin with positive slope. The motion is:
questions.explanation: Through the origin means $u = 0$; constant positive slope means constant acceleration.

questions.q: A car decelerates uniformly from 40 m/s and stops in 100 m. Its deceleration is:
A particle moving with uniform acceleration covers 40 m in the 4th second and 60 m in the 6th second. Its acceleration is:
questions.explanation: $s_n = u + \dfrac{a}{2}(2n-1)$; subtracting: $60 - 40 = \dfrac{a}{2}(11 - 7) = 2a \Rightarrow a = 10\,\text{m/s}^2$.

questions.q: From the top of a tower a stone is thrown up at 20 m/s and another dropped at the same instant. The difference in their speeds after 2 s is (g = 10 m/s$^2$):
questions.explanation: Both gain the same $gt$, so the difference in velocities stays equal to the initial difference, $20\,\text{m/s}$.

questions.q: A body travels half its total path in the last second of free fall from rest. The total time of fall is about:
questions.explanation: If total time is $t$, last-second fraction $\dfrac{1}{2}$ gives $(t-1)^2 = \dfrac{t^2}{2}$, so $t = 2 + \sqrt{2} \approx 3.4\,\text{s}$.

questions.q: On an x-t graph, a curve bending so its slope increases with time indicates:
questions.explanation: Increasing slope of $x$-$t$ means increasing velocity, i.e. positive acceleration.

questions.q: A man rows a boat at 5 m/s in still water across a river flowing at 3 m/s. Relative to the bank, considering only the downstream direction, the river carries the boat downstream at:
questions.explanation: The downstream drift is set by the river's velocity along the bank, $3\,\text{m/s}$ (the rowing is across the flow).
